Key ideas

Useful electronic components

Definitions

Diode: a semiconductor with very large resistance to current flow in one direction but very small in the other; a semiconductor device that will only allow electrical current to flow through it in one direction
Light-emitting diode (LED): a diode that lights up when current flows through it but since it is a diode current will not flow in the reverse direction
Potentiometer: a circuit device consisting of a three-terminal sliding or rotating contact (called the ‘wiper’). Connections at one end and the wiper can be used to create a variable resistor. Often used as a volume control or light dimmer.
Light dependent resistor (LDR): a semiconductor device whose resistance depends on the intensity of light shining on it
Thermistor: a thermal resistor, a non-ohmic semiconductor device whose resistance changes with temperature; two main types: NTC (negative thermal coefficient) increases RRR with decreasing temperature, is the most common type. PTC (positive thermal coefficient) increases RRR with increasing temperature, is made for special jobs.

New knowledgeDiodes and LEDs

Useful electronic components

A diode is a semiconductor made mainly of silicon, germanium or selenium and doped with impurities such as phosphorus and aluminium.

The reasons for a semiconductor’s function are beyond the scope of this course, but it is enough to say that a semiconductor conducts less well than a metal, and its resistance depends on the distribution of impurities and the temperature.

A diode is a non-ohmic resistance, and in fact its I–V characteristic is not even symmetrical: the size of the current depends on which way the potential difference is connected to the diode, or, to think of it another way, the direction of the potential difference, or polarity, affects the size of the current.

The resistance of a diode is very large in one direction, but very small in the other.

Figure 6A–2 Diodes and their symbols. Left: the banded end of a diode shows the side that should be connected facing the negative terminal of the supply potential difference, if current is to flow. Right: The circuit symbol for a diode reflects its function: the triangle is like an arrow showing the direction current can flow, and the line across the ‘nose’ of the triangle is like a wall that current cannot pass through when it approaches from that direction. This end of the diode has the band shown on left.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 66
6A

New knowledgeDiodes and LEDs: the I–V characteristic of a diode

Useful electronic components

The I–V characteristic for a diode is obtained in the same way as the circuit used in Section 5C to record the characteristic of a resistor, but after the initial set of readings the potential difference must also be reversed (you may need to reverse the ammeter and voltmeter leads if using analogue meters) to measure the current in the opposite direction.

Instead of a straight-line ohmic graph, the diode shows almost zero resistance in one direction, and a very large resistance in the other (note that the horizontal axis is not to scale).

Under normal conditions, current can only flow through a diode in one direction.

This can be useful to protect components that would be damaged by reverse current, and to change AC (alternating current) into DC (direct current); for example, in the charger for a laptop.

Figure 6A–4 Left: This circuit should look familiar from Section 5D. Right: I–V characteristic for a diode. Note that the scales in the positive and negative potential difference are not equal. The forward bias potential, $V_F$, varies depending on the semiconductor composition but is 0.6–1.0 V for silicon. When reverse biased, 50 V or more, $V_{BR}$, can be applied before the semiconductor breaks down and becomes a conductor.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 77
6A

New knowledgeDiodes and LEDs: the I–V characteristic of a diode

Useful electronic components

Use of a diode alone in a rectifier circuit (changing AC to DC) results in the conversion of only 50% of the electrical energy, as the electrical energy carried by all the ‘backwards’ current that is blocked does not transfer to the DC current.

Safety note: like any component, diodes can only dissipate a certain amount of energy before they break down (or ‘blow’).

Always check the details before you connect one.

If a diode is subject to more current or potential difference than it can handle, it will heat up, melt or smoke.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 78
6A

New knowledgeDiodes and LEDs: the I–V characteristic of a diode

Useful electronic components

Often a small value resistor is put in series with the diode for protection.

Some of the potential difference will be across the resistor, not all across the diode, and the current will be lower.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 79
6A

New knowledgeLight-emitting diode (LED)

Useful electronic components

A more easily noticed component is a light-emitting diode (LED), often seen as the ‘power on’ or ‘standby’ light on electrical appliances, and combined in lamps as an efficient replacement for filament and fluorescent household lighting.

As the name suggests and the symbol shows, the LED lights up when current flows through it (it is said to be ‘forward biased’) but not when the potential difference is reversed because, being a diode, no current will flow ‘backwards’ through it.

In the same way as the diode, the resistance of an LED is very small in one direction, but very large in the other.

The I–V characteristic of an LED can be obtained in the same way as usual, by varying the potential difference across it and recording the current through it, then reversing the polarity of the power supply and repeating the process.

Figure 6A–6c c Circuit symbol for an LED.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 810
6A

New knowledgeLight-emitting diode (LED)

Useful electronic components

A typical I–V graph for an LED is shown in Figure 6A–8.

For the same amount of light, arrays of LEDs in a mains-connected LED lamp use significantly less energy than filament bulbs or fluorescents.

They are more efficient and are becoming cheaper to produce than older technology.

LEDs and lighting are now part of the twenty-first century electrical revolution.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 811
6A

New knowledgePotentiometer (or variable resistor)

Useful electronic components

Figure 6A–9 shows different versions of a useful piece of equipment, a potentiometer (‘pot’), that can be used in a couple of different ways, and, perhaps confusingly, often gets a different name according to how it is set up in a circuit.

You might hear it called a potential divider, rheostat, variable resistor or dimmer switch.

It is basically a long wire of high resistance, often insulated and coiled for convenience, with electrical contacts or terminals at each end (terminal A and C in Figure 6A–9) and a sliding contact which can be moved to different positions along the wire.

Current flows between terminals A and B.

Figure 6A–11 Circuit symbol for a potentiometer or variable resistor
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1012
6A

New knowledgePotentiometer (or variable resistor)

Useful electronic components

See Figures 6A–12 and 6A–13 for circuit diagrams for the potentiometer in use.

The circuit symbol for a potentiometer is shown in Figure 6A–11.

You choose which two or three of the terminals to connect depending on the job you want the pot to do in the circuit.

Recall that in Section 5C you learned how two resistors in series can be used to divide up the potential difference according to the ratio of their resistances, creating a potential divider.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1013
6A

New knowledgePotentiometer (or variable resistor)

Useful electronic components

The same idea is used in a potentiometer.

The two resistors are replaced by a long piece of ohmic resistance wire with a sliding contact that can be moved to any position, from one end of the wire to the other.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1014
6A

New knowledgePotentiometer as a potential divider

Useful electronic components

Because they are made from resistance wire that obeys Ohm’s law, the proportion of the lengths of wire on each side of the sliding contact is the same as the proportion of potential difference across each end of the wire.

As seen in Figure 6A–12, the sliding contact for VoutV_{\text{out}}Vout​ moves along the wire.

If it’s half-way along, then Vout=12VV_{\text{out}} = \frac{1}{2}VVout​=21​V.

If the slider is three-quarters of the way up, then Vout=34VV_{\text{out}} = \frac{3}{4}VVout​=43​V; if it’s a quarter of the way up, then Vout=14VV_{\text{out}} = \frac{1}{4}VVout​=41​V.

Figure 6A–12 Left: A circuit diagram of a potentiometer connected to a battery, with a voltmeter connected to measure the potential difference. This type of connection to a potentiometer can be used as a dimmer for lights or as a volume control. Right: Drawing of a globe connected in place of the voltmeter, $V_{\text{out}}$.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1215
6A

New knowledgePotentiometer as a potential divider

Useful electronic components

Mathematically, we would say that the resistance is directly proportional to the length.

If you know the total resistance of the whole wire, the resistance can be obtained with simple ratios from an accurate length measurement.

For circuits with this arrangement, there is always current in the whole length of the potentiometer, and the slider can be positioned to provide varying potential difference to the output side of the circuit when a connection is made between points C and B.

Note that all three terminals are in use.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1216
6A

New knowledgePotentiometer as a potential divider

Useful electronic components

The rest of the circuit will effectively be in parallel with the section B to C of the potentiometer, so extra current flows from the power supply when a load is connected to VoutV_{\text{out}}Vout​.

The potential difference across the pot doesn’t change, nor does the current through the lower part of the potential divider (below the slider).

Any value of potential difference, VoutV_{\text{out}}Vout​, can be chosen for the load, simply by moving the slider.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1217
6A

New knowledgePotentiometer as a variable resistor (rheostat)

Useful electronic components

A second method of setting up the circuit involves deliberately controlling the current, rather than the potential difference, by using the same piece of equipment as a variable resistor (sometimes called a rheostat).

Figure 6A–13 shows that only two terminals are connected, one end (A) and the slider (B).

The longer the wire included in the circuit, the greater the resistance and the lower the current in the circuit, so moving the sliding contact directly controls the current.

The variable resistor is effectively in series with the rest of the circuit.

Figure 6A–13 A circuit diagram (left) and a drawing of the set-up for using a potentiometer (rheostat) with only two terminals connected – one end (A) and the slider (B) – to vary the current (right)
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1318
6A

New knowledgePotentiometer as a variable resistor (rheostat)

Useful electronic components

Current only flows through the part of it that is selected (A to B in this case), and both the current and the potential difference are affected when the slider is moved.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1319
6A

New knowledgeLight dependent resistor (LDR)

Useful electronic components

The light dependent resistor (LDR) is a semiconductor device whose resistance depends on the intensity of light of suitable wavelength shining on it.

The incident light might vary with the distance from a light source, or due to night falling, or because the door of a cupboard is opened.

For a particular light intensity, the LDR behaves as a resistor of constant resistance, obeying Ohm’s law over a small range of potential difference.

To obtain the I–V characteristic, it is necessary to measure and state the light level at which the potential difference and current measurements were taken.

Figure 6A–16 Left: Graph of resistance versus light intensity level (in lux, lx) for a light dependent resistor. Note the logarithmic scales on both axes. With light of low intensity of about 10 lx, $R = 10^6\ \Omega$ or 10 MΩ. With 1000 lx, the resistance is as low as 10 Ω. Right: I–V characteristic of an LDR. For a given light level, the LDR is ohmic within a given range of potential difference.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1520
6A

New knowledgeLight dependent resistor (LDR)

Useful electronic components

A more useful graph is resistance versus light level.

It is measured in units of lux (lx).

As the brightness of light increases, the resistance decreases in an exponential way.

These relationships are shown in the graphs in Figure 6A–16.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1521
6A

New knowledgeLight dependent resistor (LDR)

Useful electronic components

LDRs can be used in a range of applications; for example, in light meters or to control an automatic flash.

Streetlights or night lights that turn on as it gets dark can use an LDR in a potential divider circuit.

If a variable resistor is used, the level of light that turns on the streetlights can be altered.

A very common use of an LDR is to trigger a buzzer or an alarm when a person entering a doorway breaks a beam of light.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1522
6A

New knowledgeThermistor

Useful electronic components

The thermistor (short for ‘thermal resistor’) is another semiconductor device.

The resistance of a thermistor changes with temperature, so an I–V graph needs to specify what the temperature was when the current and potential difference were measured.

It can also show different lines on the graph for different temperatures.

For a particular temperature, most thermistors obey Ohm’s law over a small range of potential differences.

Figure 6A–18 Left: A bead-type thermistor; its resistance changes with temperature. Right: Thermistor symbol
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1723
6A

New knowledgeThermistor

Useful electronic components

The more useful graph in Figure 6A–19 shows two types of thermistors: • negative thermal coefficient thermistor (NTC): as the temperature rises, resistance falls in an exponential-like manner.

Most thermistors are this type, so you may assume a thermistor is NTC type unless stated otherwise • positive temperature coefficient thermistor (PTC): as the temperature rises, resistance suddenly rises steeply in an exponential-like manner.

These are mostly custom-designed for specific applications.

Thermistors can be used for temperature control in heaters and air conditioners, refrigerators and ovens, and in digital thermometers, among other applications.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1724
6A

New knowledgeTransducers

Useful electronic components

Devices that change one form of energy into another are called transducers.

They can be used as input to a circuit; for example, an LDR that detects the level of light (light → electrical energy) or a microphone that detects a sound and then triggers a change in the circuit (sound → electrical energy).

There are also output transducers, like the buzzer that sounds (energy given out) when a current flows in the circuit (electrical → sound energy).

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1825
6A

New knowledgeVarying the switching level in a potential divider circuit with a transducer

Useful electronic components

You have learned how a potential divider can be used with a transducer to perform a set task, but often you need to vary the level of light or temperature at which a circuit will switch on or off.

To do this, a variable resistor in one half of the potential divider is used.

This can be set by trial and error (wait until the temperature is right and adjust the rheostat until the circuit switches on or off) or using a pre-set scale (1–10 on an amplifier or 150–300°C on an oven).

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 1826

6A

We doLDR circuit

Useful electronic components
a Describe the way the output potential difference, VoutV_{\text{out}}Vout​, changes in the circuit shown operates as it gets dark.
b Describe an application for such a circuit.
Key idea · Ohm's law (study design restriction)I=VRI = \frac{V}{R}I=RV​

Working

a The LDR is acting as part of a voltage divider in this circuit (since it is wired in series with a resistor). The output voltage, VoutV_{\text{out}}Vout​, in this case is then related to the ratio of resistances of the LDR and variable resistor. As it gets darker, the resistance of the LDR increases, so VoutV_{\text{out}}Vout​ would increase, activating the switch that then turns on the spotlight.
b This kind of circuit has a number of applications. One use could be in a nightlight. If the output voltage is connected to an electronic switch that can turn on a globe, then as night falls the resistance of the LDR increases, so a greater share of the battery potential difference will appear across the LDR, which will trigger the electronic switch. The nightlight globe is powered from an external circuit, controlled by this switch.
VoutV_{\text{out}}Vout​ increases as it gets dark; e.g. a nightlight
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 16, Worked example 6A-342
6A

We doThermistor circuit

Useful electronic components
a Describe the way this NTC thermistor circuit operates as temperature increases.
b Find an application for the circuit.
Key idea · Ohm's law (study design restriction)I=VRI = \frac{V}{R}I=RV​

Working

a In this circuit the thermistor is installed as part of a potential divider. This means as temperature increases, the thermistor resistance will decrease, which in turn will increase (or decrease) the output voltage at V. The required temperature can be achieved by changing the value of the variable resistor in the top part of the potential divider. Larger resistance in the top section means a lower temperature turns off the switch and vice versa.
b This circuit could control the settings for an oven. As the required high temperature is reached, the low output voltage triggers a switch to turn off the heating circuit.
Thermistor resistance falls as temperature rises, so the output voltage across it falls; e.g. oven control
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 6, p. 18, Worked example 6A-443

Give two similarities and one difference between a diode and an LED.

Working

Diodes and LEDs are both made of a pair of semiconductors (a pn junction) and both transmit current in one direction only. The LED emits light when a current flows through it, but a diode doesn't.

You trySection 6A questions Q8

Useful electronic components
Which of the following circuits will turn on the alarm when the temperature increases, and which will turn on the alarm when temperature decreases? Explain your reasoning for how each circuit behaves when the temperature changes. (Hint: the alarm will sound when there’s sufficient change in potential difference across it to change a switch.)
How could you adjust the circuits above to enable variation in the temperature at which the alarm sounds?

Working

LH circuit: As temperature increases, resistance of the thermistor decreases, so potential difference across the top part of the potential divider circuit (the thermistor) also decrease and pd across the resistor in the bottom half increases. This means that output potential difference increases, which should turn on the alarm.
FH circuit: As temperature increases, resistance of the thermistor decreases, so potential difference across the bottom part of the potential divider circuit (the thermistor) also decreases (and pd across the resistor in the top half increases). This means that output potential difference (across the bottom section) decreases, which will not turn on the alarm.
In LH circuit: Replace the resistor with a variable resistor or rheostat. You can then dial the resistance needed to trigger the alarm at a particular temperature.

Useful electronic components
When the sun sets, a light comes on outside the front door of a house.
a Design a circuit to make this occur, using an LDR, a potential divider and an electronic switch for a spotlight across VoutV_{\text{out}}Vout​.
b Why is this more useful than a security light on a timer?

Working

a • There are several possibilities, one of which is shown below. The theory is:
• To turn on the spotlight requires increasing potential difference at the electronic switch. Assume that this output will be across the bottom half of the potential divider.
• Resistance of LDR is high in the dark, so pd across it rises as light level falls
• So put the LDR in the bottom half of the potential divider circuit.
• Using a variable resistor in the top half of the potential divider circuit allows adjustment of the specific light level at which the spotlight turns on.
[diagram: img/6A_SQ9_ans.png]
b Using an LDR ensures that the light will come on when it gets dark, which could be at different times in the evening depending on the season, and even during days which are dark and stormy.

Useful electronic components
Design a circuit to turn on the switch for a pool pump when the sun shines. Hint: connect the switch for the pump across VoutV_{\text{out}}Vout​.

Working

There are several possibilities, one of which is shown below. The theory is:
• The electronic switch requires increased pd to turn on the pump. Assume that this output will be across the bottom half of the potential divider.
• The switch is to be operated when the sun shines ie the light level changes, so choose an LDR.
• Resistance of LDR is low in the sunshine, so pd across it drops as light level rises
• So put the LDR in the top half of the potential divider circuit.
• Using a variable resistor in the bottom half of the potential divider circuit allows adjustment of the specific light level at which the pump turns on.
[diagram: img/6A_SQ10_ans.png]

Working

There are several possibilities, one of which is shown below. The theory is:
• To turn on the LED light requires and increase of potential difference. Assume that this output will be across the bottom half of the potential divider.
• The LED is to be turned when the coffee machine is hot ie the temperature changes, so choose a thermistor.
• Resistance of thermistor goes low when the temperature rises, so pd across it drops as temperature rises
• So put the thermistor in the top half of the potential divider circuit.
• Using a variable resistor in the bottom half of the potential divider circuit allows adjustment of the specific light level at which the pump turns on.

Useful electronic components
Check-in set 1 · Q1 · 6A
A diode can be used in a circuit to control the direction of applied voltage. What property of diodes is used in this application?
When an AC voltage is applied to a diode circuit, current only flows in the forward direction. Reverse polarity potential difference across a diode causes no current.
Check-in set 1 · Q2 · 6A
Explain why diodes and LEDs are often connected in a circuit in series with a small resistor.
The diode conducts current when the forward potential difference across it is about 0.7 V or higher. There is a maximum safe current (and hence potential difference) for the diode, so a small resistor is added for protection, to limit the current. The size of the resistor is chosen according to the maximum potential difference for the diode.
Check-in set 1 · Q3 · 6A
If the protective resistor is always in the circuit, why is the voltmeter in Figure 6A–7 across only the LED and not the resistor?
To obtain an I–V characteristic, the current through the LED is plotted against the potential difference applied across the LED. Including the resistor would change these results, and would effectively give the characteristic of the power supply (since the ammeter has almost no resistance, you would be measuring the output potential difference of the power supply and the current in the circuit.)

What property of LDRs make them useful in circuits?
The useful property of LDRs is that their resistance depends on the level of light, hence at different intensities light different amounts of current can be made to flow through a circuit.

Useful electronic components
Check-in set 4 · Q1 · 6A
What property of thermistors make them useful in circuits, specifically those used to control temperature?
The property of thermistors that make them useful is that they have a variable resistance which depends on the temperature of the environment they are in. This makes them very useful in circuits that control temperature, since their resistance will change with the temperature of the environment they are in making them ideal for activating air conditioners or freezer pumps.
Check-in set 4 · Q2 · 6A
List some possible real-world applications of thermistors.
Student answers will vary but could include: sensor to regulate oven temperatures, freezer temperatures, aircon or heating temperatures etc.
